Your Excellencies, Ambassadors, representatives of diplomatic missions of UN and international organizations, ladies and gentlemen, it is my pleasure to welcome you today. I thank you for joining us for this discussion on one of the most important issues facing Syria today. How do we move from displacement to stability, from tents to homes, and from emergency assistance to a life where each Syrian can regain their dignity and build their future?

Allow me to begin with a personal story.

In 2019, During one of the major waves of displacement in northern Syria, I was visiting one of the camps in rural Idlib. An elderly woman approached me and asked, "When will we return to our homes?" I had no answer. She then said, "If our return is not going to happen soon, then at least give women some privacy in the camp." Years later, In December 2024, I met the same woman again. This time, she told me confidently, "We will return." I told her to wait, but she insisted on returning to her village in rural Hama.

A.

Few days later, she called and told me, "We returned, but the house was destroyed, and the village was devastated. There is no bakery, no health center, no roads, and no services. We tried to stay, but we could not. So we returned to the camp. For me, this story summarizes the entire challenge. Return is not simply moving people from a tent back into their village. Return means that a person finds a place where they can live in dignity and stability. From this understanding came our vision of Syria without camps and zero tents.

Ladies and gentlemen, I want to be clear about what we mean by this vision.

Our goal is not to close camps. Our goal is to eliminate the need for camps. We do not want to ask a family to leave a tent only to return to a destroyed house or to a village without water, schools, health care, or job opportunities. Therefore, The guiding principle for us is clear. Return must be voluntary, safe, dignified, and sustainable. It should not disappear before a viable alternative exists. For years, camps have been a humanitarian necessity that saved the lives of Syrians, but they were always intended as a temporary solution and could not become a permanent future for an entire generation. For this reason, Presidential Decree No. 59 was issued by the President, establishing a committee chaired by the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management with the participation of relevant government institutions to work on rehabilitating affected areas and creating the conditions necessary for the return of residents. But our experience tells us that sustainable return requires four interconnected elements. First, security. There can be no safe return before landmines, unexploded ordinances, and remnants of war are removed. Second, the rehabilitation of affected areas. Removing rubble, reopening roads, and restoring infrastructure are essential prerequisites for the people's return. Third, basic services. Schools, healthcare centers, water, electricity, bakeries, and roads what make communities livable once again. Fourth, livelihoods. Even if we rebuild homes, if people cannot find employment opportunities that enable them to provide for their families, they may be forced into displacement once again. Therefore, we are not speaking only about reconstructing buildings. We are speaking about rebuilding the ability of people to live.

Ladies and gentlemen.

We know that the primary responsibility rests with us as Syrians. Syria should lead this process. Its institutions and its local communities must remain at its center. However, we should also be realistic. The scale of destruction and the accumulated needs resulting from years of war are far greater than Syria can address on its own. This is why we need a new international partnership. We do not only need the continuation of humanitarian assistance for those who still require them. We also need to begin moving from financing displacement to financing solutions. We need investment in demining and the removal of war remnants, clearing rubble, rehabilitating schools, healthcare centers, water and electricity networks. and supporting small businesses, creating employment opportunities, and revitalizing local economies. We are not asking the international community to fund the closure of camps. We are asking it to help us build the conditions that enable Syrians, on their own free will, to leave them. And this is a fundamental difference. Investing in a village to which residents to which its residents can return, in a school that welcomes their children, in a water network that serves an entire community, and in a project that generates job opportunities, is not merely a humanitarian response. It is an investment in stability. Ladies and gentlemen, seven years ago, that woman asked me, when will we return to our homes? I had no answer then. Today, I will not make promises to any Syrian family that I cannot fulfill. But what we can do is build the conditions that make return a real, safe, and sustainable option. That is what Zero Tents means to us. It is not a number we seek to announce that we have achieved, nor is it a campaign to close camps. It is a vision for a Syria in which the tent once again becomes a temporary solution, not a home. We want to extend our hands to every partner who wishes to help us achieve this goal, because the best way to end displacement is not by removing tents, but by providing the conditions allowing people to leave them behind. Thank you, and may the peace of God be upon you.

Ibrahim, your excellencies, colleagues, partners, everyone, God peace and blessings be upon you all. Because the topic is very important, we need to start from where it should end. I'll start with the recommendations from the findings, from the messages, the key messages that I hope that we all take with us from this meeting, the main key messages regarding the vision of Syria without camps. six key messages that I hope you will take with you after we leave this room, that you take them with you and think about them, because this is the essence of this vision. The first key message is ending camps, eliminating camps does not start by closing the camps, but by preparing the infrastructure in the different areas for the return of the IDPs. The second key message is addressing displacement is the backbone for recovery in Syria and for sustainable stability. We cannot have recovery, we cannot have sustainable stability without addressing the question of displacement. The third key message, we need to flip the formula. We should not think of the IDPs or the returnees as an economic burden, but rather as a point of strength. Economically, that is a leverage tool for the national economy. The fourth message, the Syrian government has the will and the determination to create a success story out of the story of internal displacement in Syria. We hope that this story is a partnership between the Syrian government and you all. Let us make an international global success story. The fifth key message is that the Syrian government has the plans, we have the projects, We have the activities, the skills for implementation. What we lack is funding and genuine partnerships. And this is what we will present to you today. The final key message, financing temporary solutions and the continued presence of IDPs in camps is not economically feasible or cost efficient if we think about it. If we want it to be cost efficient in terms of the funding, we need to develop the communities and to invest in the IDPs in their places of origin. These are the key messages, and I hope that we all can take with us when we leave this room and that we start a genuine partnership so that we can achieve a global success story regarding displacement. 14 years of displacement, as you see it. In November 2024, the numbers were that we had 12 million IDPs. 4.5 million in camps and the remaining numbers were in the host communities. What we look at now is September 2026. There are major differences because the main reason for displacement is gone. We talk now about 1,319 total camps in Syria, not only in the northern governorates. We have 1,319 total camps with a total of 167,123 families and 842,459 displaced people. The 843,000 internally displaced people have major problems that we need to address. The distribution in terms of numbers, 89% of the camps are in the northern areas, in Aleppo, Idlib, and Hama. Accordingly, the focus of the presidential decree 59 was on these main areas because the biggest number of camps is present in the northern areas. We see also, as I said, the highest concentration of displaced persons and refugees is in Idlib and Aleppo, 80% in total. As I mentioned, The minister talked about four elements that are basic for the dignified and safe return. Safety, that there are livelihood, and genuine partnership between the government and civil society organizations and international and UN organizations. The government cannot work in isolation of partnership, genuine, that is with the UN. But what we need to document and is that we all work within one national framework and that the plans that civil society organizations, as well as international and UN organizations, fulfill the vision, the government's vision, in terms of the priorities. IDPs in Syria live in four kinds of camps, either concrete camps, prefab caravans, or concrete camps with tarpaulin roof. What we want is that we want to eliminate tents by 2026. This is a goal that is achievable for all of us. I want to mention here very quickly is that we divided the areas We have 3,344 villages where we have the IDPs from. So in the decree 59, we chose 120 priority areas. Many of the sectors that we work on, and I'm sure that the partners will confirm that, telecommunication, hospitals, housing, and these are the main pillar. When we met with many of the IDPs during our visits, the IDPs are ready to go to their original villages in tents, in caravans, if they had water, sanitation, schools, as well as health care services, and there are no mines. So the formula is simple, straightforward. It requires the missing component, namely the funding. The last slide, I would like to say now that we have 1,519 projects or 18 projects. Maybe this is a big number, but these areas deserve that because they had suffered a lot of destruction as a result of the previous regime. The infrastructure is completely destroyed. Our field teams had conducted a full survey and of all the infrastructure in these areas and as such we have 1,519 projects. Now the total cost of 2 billion dollars. We have the plans, we have the projects, as well as the statistics and the data. These reflect projects that can be implemented the minute funding is available. I would like to stress and conclude that through this partnership, let's create a global success story and that displacement is possible, not managing displacement, but ending displacement, transforming IDPs from economic and social burden, IDPs and refugees, transform them into economic strength and power, not for Syria alone, but for the whole region. Excellency, Mr. Minister, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, let me first thank our Syrian colleagues and the United Nations for organizing this timely discussion. The growing gap between humanitarian needs and available resources is placing the international humanitarian system under serious pressure. We are dealing with displacement situations that are larger, more complex, and in many cases, much more protracted. For more than 15 years, as Turkey has been hosting one of the world's largest refugee populations, with almost 2.2 million Syrians under temporary protection. Since 8 December 2024, more than 737,000 Syrians have returned voluntarily to their homeland, safely, with dignity, as witnessed by UNHCR. Looking ahead, the continuation of voluntary return of displaced Syrians will depend on the stability of Syria and the international support for its recovery. With this understanding, as Turkey, we support the No Camps initiative and its objective of finding durable solutions for displaced Syrians. We know from experience that sustainable returns depend on the conditions in their homeland. People need to know that their children can go to school, that health care and other basic services are available, and that they will be able to rebuild their lives. This is why Syria's recovery and the sustainable return of displaced Syrians must go hand in hand. Turkey is supporting efforts to improve the living conditions on the ground. We are contributing to the rehabilitation of schools and healthcare facilities while supporting Syrian institutions through technical assistance and capacity building projects. Currently, health infrastructure, vocational training, capacity building, agriculture, and restoration of cultural heritage are among our key priorities in Syria. Security and safety of Syria is equally important. mines, and other remnants of war continue to threaten civilians and prevent people from returning to their homes. Turkey continues to support Syria in this field, both through bilateral and multilateral efforts. This initiative also highlights the need to move from making return possible to making it sustainable. This requires rebuilding homes and neighborhoods, restoring infrastructure, and bringing economic activity back to communities of return. We are particularly well placed to contribute to these efforts as our construction companies have extensive experience in delivering large scale housing, infrastructure, and urban development projects rapidly, efficiently, and at competitive cost. We would like to put this capacity at the service of serious reconstruction. In partnership with Syrian companies, international financial institutions, and development partners, we can help rebuild communities in a way that also creates jobs, supports local supply chains, and restores livelihoods. In this sense, we believe that investment in reconstruction is also investment in sustainable return. There is also a security dimension that should not be overlooked as camps are progressively closed. We should remain vigilant against the risk that individuals affiliated with terrorist organizations may have infiltrated or found shelter within camp populations. Ultimately, the success of the No Camps Initiative will depend on what awaits people after they leave the camps. The international community should increasingly channel its resources towards communities of return to support Syrian-led efforts to create the conditions for voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable returns. Turkey stands ready to continue working with Syria, the United Nations, international financial institutions and other partners towards this objective. I thank you.
